area: Generative AI and LLM adoption, use, value and risk in organizations (IS perspective)
gaps: Micro-to-macro translation: task-level gains of 12-40% (QJE, Management Science, Organization Science) coexist with precise nulls on hours and earnings in Denmark, 1.4% aggregate time savings in US surveys, individual-only email savings in the Copilot experiment and a perceived-versus-measured paradox among executives; no paper read reconciles them with data. Disproved by organization-level studies linking telemetry-measured use to throughput or cycle time over a year or more.

Expert-worker downside and verification labor: top performers show quality declines (Brynjolfsson et al., Alibaba) and experienced developers slow down (METR); the IS review calls for verification skills research. Disproved by field studies showing no expert quality loss under adjusted workflows or newer tools.

Behavioral measurement of shadow and undisclosed GenAI use: DART, the BYOAI maturity model, Schneider et al. and the ICIS field study are conceptual or interview-based; no public trace dataset of sanctioned versus personal-account use was found. Disproved by a published study or open dataset with such trace data.

Causal evaluation of governance-of-use mechanisms: one single-firm quasi-experiment (Leon) against many frameworks; the IS review names adaptive governance and regulatory translation as open. Disproved by multi-firm field or quasi-experiments showing which controls change behavior without large circumvention.

Artifact under-specification in IS GenAI studies: the ISJ editorial exists because of it; surveys measure generic 'GenAI use' while the same tool is used in 21%-75% of weeks across firms. Disproved by IS studies that specify model, integration mode and configuration and show results differ by them.

Trust, delegation and legitimacy of controls: trust is the strongest predictor of use in one survey and non-significant in another (Kim and Kim); perceived legitimacy is a boundary condition for guardrails. Disproved by convergent evidence that trust constructs predict use and compliance uniformly across tasks and control regimes.
contradictions: Task-level productivity gains (15-26% in field experiments) versus organization-level nulls (earnings and hours effects bounded under 2% in Denmark; 1.4% reported time savings in US surveys; no reallocation of work in the Copilot experiment).

Skill-leveling narrative versus expert harm: the same studies that show novices gaining most report small significant quality declines for top performers (QJE, Alibaba) and METR finds experienced developers 19% slower.

Perceived versus measured effects: METR developers believed they were 20% faster while 19% slower; executives' perceived gains exceed measured gains (NBER w34984); IS surveys rely on perceived usefulness.

Version and reporting inconsistencies: Dillon et al. 56 firms/over 6,000 workers (arXiv v1) versus 66 firms/7,137 workers (later abstract); Bick et al. 40%/23%/9% (NBER) versus 45%/27%/10% (Management Science); Brynjolfsson et al. 5,179 agents and 14% (SSRN) versus 5,172 and 15% (QJE); Humlum and Vestergaard's NBER paper retitled; press claims of '6,000 executives, 89% no change' do not match the w34984 abstract.
Trust as the strongest predictor of GenAI use (IJHCI snippet) versus trust not significant once habit and perceived risk are modeled (Kim and Kim, Sage Open 2026).

Semantic Scholar labels the ICIS 2025 venue 'International Conference on Interaction Sciences' and returned a mismatched abstract for Feuerriegel et al.; Crossref matched the METR paper to an unrelated ICSE 2026 article at score 0.474.

area: Retrieval-augmented generation and enterprise knowledge management
gaps: Evaluation-validity gap: enterprise RAG benchmarks (HERB, EnterpriseRAG, EnterpriseRAG-Bench, Dell judge) rely on LLM judges without chance-corrected human validation; Norman et al. and Zeng et al. show such scores can mislead, and Barnett et al. found automated and human verdicts diverge. Disproved by an enterprise benchmark reporting kappa-level human-judge agreement, position-bias audits and judge-swap sensitivity.

Cost-matched comparison gap: graph, fusion, multi-stage and agentic components are evaluated at one corpus size with unbounded budgets, while the cost-matched studies (Laitenberger, Wang, Medrano, Abdallah, Li) each find the simple option competitive or better. Disproved by cost-matched comparisons on real enterprise corpora across scales showing consistent gains.

Lab-to-practice gap in evaluation and data quality: 11 of 13 practitioners evaluate manually or not at all (Brehme), IBM reports benchmark techniques useless for novel questions (Packowski), DQ frameworks do not cover RAG (Mueller), and the Applied Sciences SLR names a lab-to-market gap. Disproved by field studies showing automated RAG evaluation adopted in organizations with measured agreement to expert judgment.

Operational/temporal gap: every benchmark found is a static snapshot although Barnett et al. say validation is only feasible in operation and practitioners re-evaluate by hand after each data change; CRUD-RAG is the only benchmark with update/delete scenarios. Disproved by published longitudinal evaluations of RAG over changing corpora with regression detection.

Abstention and consequence gap: unanswerable-query detection ranges from 6% to 64% across models on HERB, RGB's negative-rejection weakness persists, and commercial tools hallucinate 17-33% (Magesh). Disproved by studies linking calibrated abstention to measured organizational outcomes rather than benchmark accuracy.

IS/KM theory gap: the only IS-venue empirical item is an interview-based data-quality paper (ICIS 2025); KM-venue work is a UTAUT2 adoption survey and conceptual pieces (BISE catchword). Disproved by IS-journal or ICIS/ECIS empirical studies of RAG-enabled KM outcomes, which may exist because the AISeL and INFORMS domain filters failed in this scan.
contradictions: Graph RAG: Edge et al. claim substantial gains for global sensemaking; Han et al. find complementary strengths only on multi-hop; GraphRAG-Bench's abstract says GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG; in HERB GraphRAG is the worst standard method on average (10.31) yet best at detecting unanswerable queries (63.41%); Zeng et al. attribute part of reported gains to evaluation bias.

Lexical vs dense vs hybrid: HERB's best standard pipeline is a dense+BM25 hybrid; Wang et al. report BM25 alone leading at scale with dense retrieval less accurate; Medrano et al. find multi-query fusion no better than a single query once re-ranking and context budgets are fixed.

Long context vs RAG: Li et al. find LC beats RAG by 3.6-13.1 points when the corpus fits the window; HERB shows even product-scoped long context 23 points below oracle and open models collapsing (Llama-3.1-405B at 18.20); Lost in the Middle shows mid-context degradation; Barnett et al. found 8K beat 4K 'contrary to prior work'.

Fine-tuning vs RAG: Ovadia et al. and Lakatos et al. find RAG beats unsupervised/domain fine-tuning, Lakatos et al. report combining them can degrade performance, while Barnett et al. cite end-to-end training as a remedy for bespoke pipelines; blog claims of a combination advantage were excluded.

Cost priorities: practitioners rate cost and scalability low while prototyping (Brehme), whereas the architecture-relevant research results (Li, Wang, Abdallah, Medrano) are all cost-accuracy trade-offs.

Judge reliability vs judge usage: HERB generates data with GPT-4o and judges with GPT-4o, the Dell judge paper argues generic judge metrics give ambiguous signals, and Norman et al. show production judges can be both highly consistent and position-biased, yet nearly every enterprise benchmark reports LLM-judge scores as the headline metric.

area: LLM agents for enterprise workflows, business process management, intelligent automation and process mining
gaps: Process-aware evaluation of enterprise agents: the 2026 manifesto names benchmarking APM as open; TheAgentCompany, WorkArena and CRMArena-Pro evaluate outcomes or UI states without any process model, frame or conformance measure, and PM-LLM-Benchmark evaluates LLM answers rather than agent behaviour. Disproved by a published benchmark scoring agent traces by conformance to a normative/operational process model with act/defer/ask/refuse outcomes.

When LLM semantics help predictive process monitoring: Weytjens and Weber find argmax matches LLMs on most of seven logs, Padella et al. find LLM gains only with about 100 traces, Rebmann et al. find fine-tuning necessary. Disproved by a study reporting trivial, classical and LLM baselines on the same public logs across training-set sizes with a consistent result.

Evidence fidelity of LLMs on log-grounded tasks: knowledge-driven hallucination is shown for text-to-model generation but no controlled study with atypical or shuffled event logs was found. Disproved by a paper measuring how often LLM-based discovery or analysis contradicts the log in favour of a standard schema.

Field evidence on governing agents in business processes: the 22 interviewees in Vu et al. had no practical experience, IS-venue hits are a typology and a research-in-progress paper, and Kaltenpoth et al.'s process-rule result was only readable as a snippet. Disproved by case or field studies of deployed LLM agents with measured compliance, failure or rework outcomes.

Mapping agent failure modes to process deviations: Cemri et al.'s taxonomy and agent-observability preprints exist separately from conformance-checking deviation types. Disproved by a method paper classifying agent-trace deviations with process-mining constructs and relating them to reliability outcomes.

Small open-weight models for process mining under CPU constraints: PM-LLM-Benchmark finds tiny models inadequate and instruction tuning helps only on some tasks. Disproved by a benchmark showing 1-4B instruction-tuned models reach larger-model performance on semantics-aware tasks.
contradictions: Early optimism (Grohs et al. 2023; Berti and Qafari 2023 technical report) versus later controlled results: out-of-the-box LLMs struggle on semantics-aware tasks (Rebmann et al. 2025), revert to standard process schemas against evidence (Kourani, Antonov et al. 2025), and are matched by a counting argmax baseline on next-activity prediction (Weytjens and Weber 2026), while Padella et al. report LLM wins only in data-scarce settings.

Manifestos frame agents as first-class, norm-governed process participants, but the benchmarks that actually measure agents contain no process model or conformance notion, and the process-mining benchmarks evaluate LLM answers rather than agents acting in processes.

Practitioners expect compliance benefits from agents (Vu et al. 2025) while CRMArena-Pro measures near-zero inherent confidentiality awareness and a trade-off between prompting for it and task performance.

Venue metadata disagree: Semantic Scholar/DBLP and Crossref list TheAgentCompany and Cemri et al. as NeurIPS 2025 while the arXiv records say Preprint; Crossref gives 2025 issued and 2026 print years for BPM 2025 chapters; Crossref's best matches for WorkArena and CRMArena-Pro were wrong items and were rejected.

area: LLM-based decision support and business analytics
gaps: Gap 1: benchmark validity to deployment validity. Enterprise accuracies of 5.7-23% (Spider 2.0), 10.8% (BEAVER) and annotation error rates above 50% (Jin et al.) coexist with production-readiness claims (NL2SQL360); no paper seen links benchmark error to downstream decision error. Reliance experiments use labels, search answers or diagrams (Cecil, Spatharioti, Anthis); none presents SQL-derived tables or charts with injected errors; forward citations of Spider 2.0 and BIRD are almost entirely model-side. Disproved by finding experiments in which participants audit LLM-generated query results or dashboards with known errors.

Gap 3: direction of the LLM-advice effect in business forecasting. Positive (Schoenegger), null-to-negative (Abolghasemi; HBR press item) results on different task types; Tan et al. undermine the model-side claim. Disproved by an IJF/EJOR experiment giving forecasters LLM advice on demand series with promotions against no-aid and statistical-aid controls.

Gap 4: ambiguity, calibration and abstention as a human factor in NL-to-data interfaces. SQUAB, the EMNLP calibration paper, Lee (2026 preprint) and Wu (2026 preprint) are model- or architecture-side; no study tests whether confidence display, clarification or abstention changes user decisions. Disproved by a user study manipulating these and measuring reliance and accuracy.

Gap 5: a validated measure of decision quality for analytics agents. InsightBench uses planted insights and an LLM judge; AoR exists only for advice-taking; Lee's Business Truth Rate and Argo-Bench's consequence grading (both 2026 preprints) score agents on synthetic warehouses, not human decisions. Disproved by a validated instrument scoring analytics output by the decision a person makes with it.

Gap 6: small open models under enterprise schema scale and the cost-value trade-off. Spider 2.0 tests 72B-405B open models only; Tan et al. show LLM components cost orders of magnitude more compute for no forecasting gain; Lee's 7B rule-gated agent narrows but does not close the gap (synthetic data, no ablation). Nothing seen evaluates 1-4B quantised models on Spider 2.0-lite, corrected BIRD Mini-Dev or BEAVER. Disproved by a paper or leaderboard entry reporting such models on these sets. Most testable from this CPU-only session via BIRD Mini-Dev and the corrected BIRD subset.
contradictions: Gruver et al. (NeurIPS 2023) report zero-shot LLMs matching or exceeding purpose-built forecasters, whereas Tan et al. (NeurIPS 2024) find the LLM component adds nothing in three adapter-based methods; regimes differ (frozen zero-shot prompting vs fine-tuned backbones, different datasets) and neither evaluates business series with promotions.

Schoenegger et al. find LLM assistants raise human forecasting accuracy by 24-28% (even a noisy assistant helps), while the HBR executive study (press-level evidence) reports ChatGPT made managers more optimistic and less accurate and Abolghasemi et al. find LLMs alone not consistently better than humans; task type and comparison condition differ.

Schemmer et al. report explanations shift appropriateness of reliance; Cecil et al. find heatmaps and charts do not reduce overreliance; Spatharioti et al. find colour-coded highlighting does help; a Behaviour & Information Technology 2025 snippet says verbal explanations increase overreliance; format and error localisation matter more than explanation per se.

BIRD's 92.96% human reference and all leaderboard scores were computed against gold queries that Jin et al. find erroneous in about half of audited cases; Spider 2.0's claim that the lite setting is not easier, and BEAVER's changing dataset sizes across arXiv versions, mean headline accuracies are not stable quantities.

area: Human-AI collaboration, algorithmic management and AI-enabled workplace/employee monitoring
gaps: AI-specific monitoring (productivity scoring, emotion AI, LLM-based evaluation) is absent from pooled evidence: the Ravid et al. corpus ends February 2021, Vaccaro et al. cover lab decision and creation tasks, and the only AI-manager experiment (Dong et al., AIES 2025) is a single simulated-workplace study. Disproved by a 2024-2026 meta-analysis or multi-site field study of AI-based EPM showing effects indistinguishable from classic EPM.

Human oversight of monitoring systems is mandated (EU AI Act framing in Schauer et al., Heimbach et al.) but under-tested: one preliminary lab experiment supports it, one interview study finds it nominal, the largest meta-analysis finds human-final-decision designs lose in decision tasks, and the only regulation-in-practice study covers US scheduling. Disproved by field experiments or audits showing oversight configurations robustly change fairness or worker outcomes.

Monitoring exposure is measured by self-report perception, not system telemetry: the quantitative worker-side studies use scales (COMAMA is the first validated one found) and none links logged monitoring intensity to outcomes; Kala and Lyons have objective output only for short online tasks. Disproved by a body of studies pairing monitoring-system logs with worker outcomes.

Transparency is treated as a single construct although studies reach different conclusions: Ravid et al. (positive attitudes), Cram et al. (no mitigation of threat technostress), Arunkumar et al. (non-monotonic 'murky middle'), Kala and Lyons (justification matters). Disproved by an experiment or measurement paper that separates purpose justification, mechanism explanation and contestability and shows they behave alike.

Evidence is concentrated in gig and warehouse work while the OECD employer survey shows common AM use in standard firms; remote-employee evidence is one Reddit-based CSCW paper and one NBER working paper. Disproved by a set of peer-reviewed studies of AI monitoring in standard employment with comparable designs (NTWE 2025 items by Reimann and Dupuis, seen only as titles, should be read first).
contradictions: Transparency as remedy: Ravid et al. find transparent monitoring improves attitudes; Cram et al. find perceived transparency does not mitigate threat technostress; Arunkumar et al. (preprint) find partial interpretability is worst; Sum et al. report managers withholding details to reduce anxiety while workers say opacity worsens it.

Human oversight: Schauer et al. (preliminary) find oversight improves decision performance and trust; Oezdemir et al. find supervisors' oversight becomes nominal; Vaccaro et al. find human-AI combinations underperform the better party in decision tasks with humans making the final call in over 95% of designs.

Algorithm appreciation versus aversion: Logg et al. show lay people prefer algorithmic advice, but Moritz and Schmidt and Klöpper and Messer (ECIS 2024) show being managed or rewarded by an algorithm lowers justice and trust and raises retaliation, while Dong et al. show harsher AI evaluation being accepted without demotivation.

Field versus laboratory: the two field experiments (Chan et al.; Kala and Lyons) find configuration- and framing-dependent effects, whereas vignette studies in Ravid's corpus show the most negative attitude effects (vignette rho = -.32 vs non-experiment rho = .00 for broad attitudes).

Platform versus employment: IS-journal anchors (Möhlmann et al.; Cram et al.) study Uber, while recent CSCW and economics evidence (Sum et al.; Kala and Lyons) studies remote employees; transfer of gig findings to employer-employee monitoring is asserted by reviews more than tested.

area: Explainability, fairness, reliability, AI governance, auditing and regulatory compliance in enterprise AI
gaps: Outcome evidence for audit mandates is missing: LL 144 studies (Wright, Groves, Gerchick, Hilliard) show low observable compliance and incomplete, probably publication-biased audits, and no published causal study links an audit mandate to hiring, lending or incident outcomes; a peer-reviewed difference-in-differences or regulator-data study would disprove it.

No validated instrument measures organizational AI governance effectiveness: tools are rarely validated (Kuehnert), evaluations measure usability not effectiveness (Berman), reviews find few complete frameworks (Batool), and IS case and maturity studies (Papagiannidis, Heger, Mäntymäki) stop at dimensions; an IS scale with predictive validity against audit findings or incidents would disprove it.

Deployer-side and SME operationalization of the EU AI Act is studied only at single-organization or perception level (Jarvers, Wagner, Lai, Schrader) and automated compliance checkers give false assurance (Tao); a multi-organization longitudinal study of deployer compliance workflows after August 2026 would disprove it.

Regulatory explanation duties lack field evidence that explanations improve decision-makers' objective understanding or contestability in HR and credit (Bhatt, Kalff and Simbeck, Ioannou, Van den Berg); in-firm field experiments showing objective-understanding or contestation gains would disprove it.

Documentation and audit reports are used as assurance evidence without evidence of their reliability (Lam's indirect verification and Raji's design history file versus shallow model cards in Liang and Bhat and incomplete LL 144 audits in Gerchick); studies showing documentation quality predicts audit findings or incidents, or audit protocols that detect misstatement at known rates, would disprove it.

Comparative institutional design of accountability regimes is under-studied: supervision-driven fair lending (Black) versus transparency-driven LL 144 versus EU conformity assessment (Lacmanovic and Skare, public reports only; Burnat and Davidson, untested model); cross-regime empirical comparisons of firm behavior would disprove it.
contradictions: Internal audits (Raji 2020) are justified by insider access but share organizational interests; external criterion audits (Lam 2024, Raji 2022) promise independence but depend on auditee documentation and face opinion shopping; Schiff et al.'s auditors describe audits that skip external reporting, so neither model operates as described.

LL 144 requires an audit but no outcome threshold; Wright et al. and Hilliard et al. argue for floors or process coverage, while Black et al. find that supervision rather than any published threshold drove fair-lending practice, so the field disagrees on what the audited quantity should be.

Regulation demands explanations sufficient to understand and contest decisions, yet Kalff and Simbeck find XAI can reduce HR managers' objective understanding while raising trust, Bhatt et al. find explanations built for engineers, and Ioannou et al. find positive adoption effects conditional on advisor type and risk.

Kozodoi et al. show credit-scoring discrimination can be reduced at low profit cost, but Black et al. find institutional testing practice varies widely and is driven by business incentives and legal uncertainty, locating the constraint in organizations rather than algorithms.

Paul and Nandy claim governance-as-code reproduces a manual audit and cuts labor by about 75% on two deployments, whereas Tao et al. find twelve compliance checkers foster a false sense of compliance and Langer et al. argue human-oversight compliance resists checklists.

Audit frameworks rely on auditee documentation as evidence, while Liang et al. and Bhat et al. show limitation and evaluation sections are the least complete and Liang et al.'s intervention suggests documentation is incentivized by download visibility rather than accountability.

gaps: G1. Judge validation standards for domain tasks: raw agreement dominates validation although chance-corrected agreement is 33-41 points lower and judge rankings do not transfer across benchmarks (2026 cohort preprint); no record received tests whether small CPU-runnable open judges pass a chance-corrected, calibrated validation on IS-style artefacts. Disproved by a paper reporting kappa and calibrated CIs for 1-4B judges on MT-bench, LLMBar or JUDGE-BENCH or on IS artefacts.

G2. Preference leakage and self-preference in same-family generate-and-judge pipelines: Preference Leakage, Wataoka et al. and Panickssery et al. establish the effect for frontier models, but no record measures it for small open judges from the same family as the generator, which is the setting a no-API project would use. Disproved by a small-scale cross-family leakage study or evidence that perplexity-based familiarity is negligible below some size.

G3. Statistical and reporting practice audit for LLM evaluations in IS and BISE venues: Miller, Bowyer et al. and Lee et al. give recommendations and Bean et al. audit 445 CS benchmarks, but domain-filtered searches (queries 9-14, 24) returned no IS hits. Disproved by an existing IS meta-research paper auditing error bars, repeated runs, judge validation or model-version reporting.

G4. Contamination and nondeterminism as threats to IS evaluation claims: TS-Guessing, training-on-the-test-task adjustment and N-run variance protocols exist, but none of the records applies them to the business-process or enterprise datasets used in IS papers. Disproved by a study running contamination probes or repeated-run variance on such datasets.

G5. Enterprise-document prompt injection at small scale: Liu et al.'s resume-screening example, AgentDojo, ASB and NetInjectBench cover consumer, finance and network domains, and Nasr et al. show static evaluations over-claim; no benchmark received covers HR, monitoring or internal-document pipelines with small open backbones and adaptive attackers. Disproved by a domain benchmark covering enterprise documents or evidence that AgentDojo results transfer unchanged.

G6. Sycophancy of the judge toward the submitter: Sharma et al., SycEval, CALM and Chen et al. document agreement, authority and bandwagon effects in generation and judging, but none of the records tests whether a verdict shifts when the artefact's author asserts quality, seniority or a prior rating; two 2026 preprints seen as titles only (AMEL, Jagged Judges) may cover it. Disproved by reading those or by a null result.
contradictions: Validation metric: Zheng et al. and most follow-ups validate judges with raw agreement, while 'Reliability without Validity' (2026 preprint) and Lee et al. (ICML 2026) argue raw agreement overstates discrimination by 33-41 points and require chance correction or calibration sets; the field has not converged on a standard.

Error bars: Miller 2024 recommends CLT standard errors with clustering, whereas Bowyer et al. (ICML 2025 position paper) show CLT intervals are badly anti-conservative below a few hundred items, which covers MT-bench (80 questions) and JudgeBench (350 pairs); compatible in principle but applied work rarely states which regime it is in.

Verbosity bias: Zheng et al. report 91.3% failure of Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 under a repetitive-list attack, while the 2026 cohort study reports verbosity bias as small (<0.011) under a single pairwise rubric; the sources received do not resolve whether newer judges changed or the designs differ.

Self-preference as harm: Wataoka et al. and Panickssery et al. frame self-preference as bias, while 'Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason?' (2025 preprint, abstract only) asks whether it reflects genuinely better outputs on verifiable tasks.

Position bias cause: Zheng et al. speculate it is architectural or data-driven; Shi et al. (IJCNLP-AACL 2025) find it is driven mainly by the quality gap between candidates and only weakly by length, suggesting tie-breaking behaviour rather than a fixed prior.

Honesty vs truthfulness: MASK argues prior truthfulness benchmarks measure accuracy rather than honesty, so earlier 'honesty' results are not comparable with its own (a construct-validity dispute, not conflicting measurements).

Verification metadata: Crossref offered the same Findings of EMNLP 2025 DOI (10.18653/v1/2025.findings-emnlp.510) for both Preference Leakage (0.451) and Self-Preference Bias (0.673); both cannot be right, so both stay labelled preprint.

area: Efficient and private AI for resource-constrained organizations and underserved languages
gaps: Gap 1: no study found evaluating quantized small models (1-4B) on Bangla, Swahili or Indonesian organizational text tasks under CPU constraints; existing disparate-harm evidence (Marchisio et al.; Marie and Fujita) uses MMLU-style and MT benchmarks on languages the models already support. Disproved if Miranda et al.'s 232-paper survey or the LowResNLP 2025 workshop contains such an evaluation.

Gap 2: no peer-reviewed, costed CPU-only deployment frontier (quality per dollar or per watt) for SMEs or public bodies in developing economies; Khalil et al. use an RTX 5090 and Pan et al. assume GPU servers and subscription pricing. Disproved by a CPU-only TCO study with measurements for small organizations, possibly in systems venues not domain-filtered here.

Gap 3: country-level language effects on adoption (Misra et al.; Daepp and Slaughter) and firm-level SME adoption models (Kasigit et al.; Mohammed et al.) do not connect; no firm-level study includes local-language model performance or on-premise deployability as a construct. Disproved by an IS study in EJISDC, ITD or ISF with such constructs.

Gap 4: the contradiction between Borgersen and Goodwin's null result (GGUF, 70B, Norwegian) and the disparate-harm findings (GPTQ/AWQ/bitsandbytes and multiple formats, 1.7B-103B, non-Latin scripts) is unresolved; no factorial replication crossing quantizer family, model size (1-8B) and script on the same tasks was found. Feasible on this project's CPU-only hardware.

Gap 5: no locally grounded public-sector or SME-task benchmark for Bangla, Swahili or Indonesian comparable to MÖVE (German) or the Dutch government benchmark; SOMAJGYAAN covers Bangla culture and social knowledge only. Disproved if such a benchmark exists on the ACL Anthology or Hugging Face.
contradictions: Borgersen and Goodwin 2025 find non-significant effects of calibration language under GGUF k-quantization (Llama 3.3 70B, English and Norwegian), whereas Marchisio et al. 2024 and Marie and Fujita 2025 report larger degradation for non-Latin-script and low-resource languages and for smaller models; the studies differ in quantizer family, model size, script and metric, and Marie and Fujita's finding that GGUF is the most robust format partially reconciles them.

Khalil et al. 2025 frame their single-GPU server as comparable to cloud services, but their own results show per-request efficiency falling 75% from one to two concurrent users and no cost figures appear in the text despite the SMB-affordability claim.

Misra et al. 2025 conclude that more training data is the only solution, while TigerLLM claims a 1B-class Bangla model already beats GPT-3.5 and Mahfuz et al. argue dedicated Bengali LLMs are needed but the data to build them are lacking.

IS adoption studies (Kasigit et al.; Mohammed et al.) explain SME non-adoption with finance, skills and infrastructure and no language or compute variables, while CS studies explain capability gaps with no organizational variables; the reference lists of the three central papers show no cross-citation between the strands.

Marchisio et al. show automatic metrics understate quantization harm by roughly an order of magnitude relative to human evaluation, yet the deployment and efficiency papers in this set rely on automatic benchmarks alone.
